title: Light and Reflection
seo_title: Grade 10 Science (SNC2D): Light and Reflection Worksheets (Ontario)
standard_text: The properties and sources of light; the electromagnetic spectrum; the laws of reflection; images in plane mirrors; and images formed by concave and convex mirrors, using ray diagrams and the mirror and magnification equations. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 9 and 10: Science (2008), Science, Grade 10, Academic (SNC2D), Strand E: Light and Geometric Optics)
meta_desc: Free Grade 10 Science (SNC2D) worksheets on light and reflection: sources of light, the electromagnetic spectrum, the law of reflection, plane mirrors, concave and convex mirrors and the mirror equation. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection, measured from the normal.
body_html:
How to think about it

Light travels in straight lines at 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum. Visible light is a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum, between infrared and ultraviolet. When light reflects, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

A plane mirror makes a virtual, upright image the same size as the object and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. A concave (converging) mirror can make real or virtual images; a convex (diverging) mirror always makes a smaller, upright, virtual image. Use 1/f = 1/d₀ + 1/dᵢ and M = hi/ho = −dᵢ/d₀.

Example

A ray hits a mirror at 35° to the normal. Angle of reflection?

Equal to the angle of incidence

Answer: 35°

Example

A concave mirror has f = 10 cm. An object is 30 cm away. Image distance?

1/dᵢ = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30

Answer: 15 cm

Common mistakes

  • Measuring angles from the mirror surface instead of the normal.
  • Thinking an image in a plane mirror is on the mirror's surface.
  • Forgetting that convex mirrors only make virtual images.

items.q: Which describes the image formed by a plane mirror?

items.q: An object 5 cm tall is 36 cm from a convex mirror (f = −15 cm). How tall is the image? (A negative height means inverted.)
items.e: dᵢ = −10.6 cm, M = −dᵢ/d₀ = 0.294, so hᵢ = M × h₀ = 1.47 cm.

items.q: An object is 40 cm in front of a convex mirror with a focal length of −25 cm. Use 1/f = 1/d₀ + 1/dᵢ to find the image distance dᵢ.
items.e: 1/dᵢ = 1/f − 1/d₀ = 1/(−25) − 1/40, so dᵢ = −15.4 cm. A negative dᵢ is a virtual image.

items.q: A concave mirror (f = 30 cm) forms an image of an object placed 15 cm away. What is the magnification? (M = −dᵢ/d₀)
items.e: dᵢ = −30 cm, so M = −dᵢ/d₀ = −(−30) ÷ 15 = 2. M is positive: the image is upright.

items.q: An object is 30 cm in front of a concave mirror with a focal length of 15 cm. Use 1/f = 1/d₀ + 1/dᵢ to find the image distance dᵢ.
items.e: 1/dᵢ = 1/f − 1/d₀ = 1/(15) − 1/30, so dᵢ = 30 cm. A positive dᵢ is a real image.

items.q: An object is 6 cm in front of a concave mirror with a focal length of 25 cm. Use 1/f = 1/d₀ + 1/dᵢ to find the image distance dᵢ.
items.e: 1/dᵢ = 1/f − 1/d₀ = 1/(25) − 1/6, so dᵢ = −7.89 cm. A negative dᵢ is a virtual image.

items.q: A concave mirror forms an image 6 cm in front of the mirror (real) when the object is 30 cm away. What is the focal length?
A concave mirror forms an image 30 cm in front of the mirror (real) when the object is 6 cm away. What is the focal length?
An object is 24 cm in front of a convex mirror with a focal length of −10 cm. Use 1/f = 1/d₀ + 1/dᵢ to find the image distance dᵢ.
items.e: 1/dᵢ = 1/f − 1/d₀ = 1/(−10) − 1/24, so dᵢ = −7.06 cm. A negative dᵢ is a virtual image.

items.q: A convex mirror forms an image 7.83 cm behind the mirror (virtual) when the object is 36 cm away. What is the focal length?
An object is 18 cm in front of a convex mirror with a focal length of −25 cm. Use 1/f = 1/d₀ + 1/dᵢ to find the image distance dᵢ.
items.e: 1/dᵢ = 1/f − 1/d₀ = 1/(−25) − 1/18, so dᵢ = −10.5 cm. A negative dᵢ is a virtual image.

items.q: An object is 40 cm in front of a concave mirror with a focal length of 12 cm. Use 1/f = 1/d₀ + 1/dᵢ to find the image distance dᵢ.
items.e: 1/dᵢ = 1/f − 1/d₀ = 1/(12) − 1/40, so dᵢ = 17.1 cm. A positive dᵢ is a real image.

items.q: A concave mirror (f = 12 cm) forms an image of an object placed 20 cm away. What is the magnification? (M = −dᵢ/d₀)
items.e: dᵢ = 30 cm, so M = −dᵢ/d₀ = −(30) ÷ 20 = −1.5. M is negative: the image is inverted.

items.q: A concave mirror forms an image 60 cm in front of the mirror (real) when the object is 15 cm away. What is the focal length?
An object is 50 cm in front of a convex mirror with a focal length of −10 cm. Use 1/f = 1/d₀ + 1/dᵢ to find the image distance dᵢ.
items.e: 1/dᵢ = 1/f − 1/d₀ = 1/(−10) − 1/50, so dᵢ = −8.33 cm. A negative dᵢ is a virtual image.

items.q: A convex mirror (f = −20 cm) forms an image of an object placed 36 cm away. What is the magnification? (M = −dᵢ/d₀)
items.e: dᵢ = −12.9 cm, so M = −dᵢ/d₀ = −(−12.9) ÷ 36 = 0.357. M is positive: the image is upright.

items.q: A concave mirror forms an image 45 cm in front of the mirror (real) when the object is 36 cm away. What is the focal length?
A concave mirror forms an image 11.2 cm in front of the mirror (real) when the object is 9 cm away. What is the focal length?
An object is 15 cm in front of a concave mirror with a focal length of 25 cm. Use 1/f = 1/d₀ + 1/dᵢ to find the image distance dᵢ.
items.e: 1/dᵢ = 1/f − 1/d₀ = 1/(25) − 1/15, so dᵢ = −37.5 cm. A negative dᵢ is a virtual image.

items.q: An object 5 cm tall is 40 cm from a concave mirror (f = 8 cm). How tall is the image? (A negative height means inverted.)
items.e: dᵢ = 10 cm, M = −dᵢ/d₀ = −0.25, so hᵢ = M × h₀ = −1.25 cm.
